questions.question: In an on-premises environment, who is responsible for replacing a failed hard disk in a server?

options.text: The organisation that owns the server
options.why: Correct. On-premises, the organisation owns and maintains all hardware.
Microsoft maintains hardware in Azure datacenters, not in your building.
ISPs provide connectivity, not server maintenance.

options.text: Nobody. Disks do not fail on-premises

questions.explanation: On-premises means you own the full stack, including physical hardware maintenance.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares on-premises and cloud capacity?

options.text: On-premises capacity can be increased in minutes; cloud capacity takes weeks
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.text: On-premises capacity is fixed until more hardware is bought; cloud capacity can be changed on demand
options.why: Correct. This is a core difference.
On-premises capacity is limited by the hardware you own.

options.text: Cloud capacity can never be reduced once added
options.why: You can scale in or delete resources at any time.

questions.explanation: Cloud capacity is provisioned on demand. On-premises capacity is limited by what you have purchased and installed.

questions.question: Which TWO costs are typically part of running an on-premises datacenter but are handled by the provider in the public cloud?

options.why: Correct. The provider pays for datacenter power and cooling.

options.text: Deciding who in your company can access your data
options.why: Access to your data and identities is always the customer's responsibility.
Correct. Hardware refresh is the provider's job in the cloud.
Data classification remains the customer's responsibility.

questions.explanation: Physical concerns (power, cooling, hardware) move to the provider. Data and access stay with you.

questions.scenario: A factory's control software must respond to machines in under 2 milliseconds and the internet link is unreliable.
questions.question: Where should this control software most likely run?

options.text: In a distant public cloud region
options.why: Network latency and an unreliable link make a remote region a poor fit.
Correct. Ultra-low latency to local equipment is a classic reason to stay on-premises or at the edge.
SaaS email is unrelated to machine control.
It can run locally, possibly managed with hybrid tools such as Azure Arc.

questions.explanation: Latency-critical, site-bound workloads are a strong case for on-premises or edge, often managed in a hybrid model.
